d.title: The whole model is five things, and three of them are from module 4
d.caption: Nothing in the implementation is new at this point — **the embedding and positional tables are 4.2, the blocks are 4.7, and the output projection is the token embedding transposed** (which is §02's weight tying). Which is the useful thing to notice before writing it: **a GPT is a decoder stack with a tied output head, and every decision inside it has already been measured** — so the parts that can go wrong are the plumbing, which is §03.

d.title: Weight tying is 38,597,376 parameters, or 31% of the model
d.caption: **The implementation hits the real checkpoint exactly — 124,439,808 — and without tying it would be 163,037,184.** The saving is precisely the token embedding table from 4.10, counted once instead of twice. And the justification is not only size: **the input embedding maps a token to a vector and the output projection maps a vector to a token, so tying them asserts the two directions use one space** — which is why untying usually does not help even when you can afford it.

d.title: Two errors that say nothing about what is wrong
d.caption: Both are real messages from writing this model, and **neither names the mistake.** The first arrives from `.view()` after a transpose — **the tensor is no longer contiguous, so the fix is `.reshape()`, and the message tells you about memory strides rather than about attention heads.** The second is an index error from `top-k` with `k` larger than the vocabulary. **Which is the practical lesson of writing a transformer by hand: the errors are tensor-shape errors, and the stack trace points at the line after the mistake.**

d.title: A loss that stops at 1.01, and 100% exact match
d.caption: The task is chosen so accuracy is unambiguous: **emit eight digits reversed, which requires attending from output position `L+1+i` back to input position `L−1−i` — a reversed copy no bigram or positional heuristic can fake.** **152,000 parameters, 36.6 seconds on CPU, 50/50 exact match.** And the loss curve is worth reading: **it reaches 1.03 by step 200 and then barely moves, flattening at 1.0106** — which is the loss on the padding and separator positions, not a failure to learn.

d.title: One head of four does the copy, at weight 0.698
d.caption: Output position 9 must copy input position 7, and **only head 2 does it — 0.698 on position 7, while heads 0 and 1 sit on position 3 and head 3 attends to itself.** Which is 4.4's finding in a model small enough to verify completely: **the task is solved by one head, the other three are doing something else or nothing, and the clean division of labour exists in exactly one of the four.** A 100% accurate model does not need all its heads to be interpretable.

d.title: Every decoding setting got it exactly right, including T=2.0
d.caption: **T=1.0 k=1, T=1.0 k=5, T=2.0 k=10 and T=0.5 k=50 all produce the exact target** — which is not a statement about decoding but about the model: **when the next token is genuinely determined, the distribution is peaked enough that flattening it by a factor of two changes nothing.** Decoding settings matter when the model is uncertain, **so a task with one correct answer is exactly the task where they do not** — and tuning them on such a task teaches you nothing.

d.title: Two operations, and the order they compose in
d.caption: **Temperature divides the logits before the softmax, so `T < 1` sharpens and `T > 1` flattens — and it never changes the ranking.** Top-k masks everything outside the `k` highest logits to `-inf`, **so the softmax assigns them exactly zero** (4.5's underflow argument again). **The two compose in that order: temperature reshapes the distribution, then top-k truncates it** — which matters, because truncating first and then flattening would redistribute mass across a set already chosen.

d.title: Four arguments, and the first one is the usual cause of a destroyed fine-tune
d.caption: **`learning_rate=2e-5` is two orders below training from scratch, and leaving it too high is the single most common cause of a fine-tune that destroys the pretrained weights.** `warmup_ratio=0.1` matters most for Post-LN models — 4.6 measured **1.918e-07 of gradient reaching the first block.** Prefer **`bf16` over `fp16` on Ampere or newer: same speed, far better dynamic range, and it avoids the loss-scaling failures.** And eval batch size can exceed training's, **because evaluation stores no gradients or optimiser state.**

d.title: Rank 8 on query and value is 0.271% of BERT
d.caption: **Freeze `W`, learn `BA` instead — and at inference fold `BA` back into `W`, so there is no added latency at all**, unlike adapters which insert real layers. The reduction is steep and the useful range is the top of the table: **rank 8 on one 768×768 projection is 12,288 parameters, a 48× reduction.** Applied to query and value across all 12 BERT layers plus a classification head: **296,450 trainable of 109,483,778 — 0.271%.**

d.title: The weights are unchanged — it is the gradients and Adam state that vanish
d.caption: **437.9 MB of weights either way. What LoRA removes is 437.9 MB of gradients and 875.9 MB of Adam state, taking the total from 1751.7 MB to 441.5 MB** — a 4× reduction, and notice **the ratio is 4× rather than 370× even though only 0.271% of parameters are trainable.** Which is the thing to understand before expecting more: **the frozen base still has to be in memory, so LoRA removes the optimiser's footprint and not the model's.**

d.title: A rank-64 truncation captures 14.5% of a random matrix, not most of it
d.caption: **LoRA is often explained as “weight matrices are low-rank”, and that claim is easy to test: a rank-64 truncated SVD of a random 768×768 matrix captures 14.5%, and rank 256 captures 49%.** So a random matrix is emphatically **not** low-rank — which means **the justification cannot be that weights are low-rank. It is that the *update* needed for a downstream task is low-rank**, which is a different and much weaker claim, and the one the empirical results actually support.

d.title: Four methods, and only one of them is free at inference
d.caption: The inference column is the differentiator. **LoRA folds `BA` into `W`, so it costs nothing at serving time.** Adapters insert bottleneck layers between blocks — **real added latency, on every forward pass, forever.** And both prompt-side methods **lengthen the effective sequence**, which is a quadratic cost under 4.3 rather than a constant one. **Prompt tuning is the cheapest to train at ~0.01% and the most fragile**, because a few thousand parameters is not much room.

d.title: Temperature 2.0 is where the teacher starts saying something useful
d.caption: At `T = 1` the teacher's distribution is `cat 0.7163` and almost nothing else — **little more information than the hard label.** At `T = 2` it says `tiger 0.2372, lion 0.2042, car 0.0412`: **cats are like tigers and lions and unlike cars, which is the knowledge being distilled.** The `T²` factor is not cosmetic — **gradients through a softmax at temperature `T` scale as `1/T²`, so without it raising the temperature would silently shrink the distillation term and `α` would stop meaning what you set.**

d.title: A Conv2d with stride equal to its kernel is the entire vision-specific part
d.caption: **`Conv2d(768, 3, 16, 16)` with kernel (16,16) and stride (16,16) does not slide — it tiles**, so it is a per-patch linear projection written as a convolution. That one line is how pixels become tokens, and **everything after it is a text transformer.** The shapes say the rest: **(1, 3, 224, 224) in, (1, 197, 768) out — 196 patches plus one `[CLS]`** — and the positional table is **(1, 197, 768)**, learned and one-dimensional over a flattened 2-D grid.

state: and the rest is a text encoder

d.title: Embeddings are 0.9% of ViT and 31.2% of GPT-2 small
d.caption: **The MLP dominates, exactly as in any transformer — 2,359,296 per `fc1` and per `fc2`, twelve times over.** The interesting number is the comparison: **ViT's entire embedding apparatus is 742,656 parameters, 0.9% of the model, against GPT-2 small's token embedding alone at 31.2%.** The reason is structural: **a vocabulary needs one row per token type and patches need none at all** — so ViT spends nothing on an input table and everything on the encoder.

d.title: Four times the resolution is 254 times the attention entries
d.caption: **224×224 gives 197 tokens and 38,809 attention entries per head per layer; 896×896 gives 3,137 tokens and 9,840,769.** Which is 4.3's quadratic term arriving as a product decision rather than a sequence-length one: **in vision you choose the sequence length by choosing the resolution and the patch size, so a “better image” is a quadratically more expensive forward pass** — and it is why high-resolution ViTs use windowed or hierarchical attention instead.

d.title: Three priors given up, and the crossover where that becomes a gain
d.caption: **Locality: a 3×3 convolution can only see neighbours, while ViT's layer-1 attention is unconstrained over all 38,809 pairs — nothing tells it adjacent patches are related. Translation equivariance: one kernel slides everywhere, so a feature found in one place is found in all; ViT must learn that per position. Hierarchy: a CNN's receptive field grows with depth, while every ViT layer is global from the start.** And the trade shows up as a data threshold: **ResNet wins at 1.3M images, equal at 14M, ViT wins clearly at 300M.**

d.title: Everything vision-specific lives in the first ten lines
d.caption: **The encoder is the same encoder — same multi-head attention, same Pre-LN blocks, same FFN at 4× width, same `[CLS]` pooling as BERT** — and the rows that differ are all about how the input becomes tokens. Which is the striking claim of ViT, and it is checkable: **two rows say “identical”.** The one row with a real asymmetry is positional encoding: **ViT uses a learned 1-D table over a flattened 2-D grid**, so the model is not told which patches are vertically adjacent.

state: set by resolution and patch size

d.title: Twenty-four characters, five tokens, no special tokens at all
d.caption: **GPT-2 is a causal LM, so there is no `[CLS]` or `[SEP]` to mark** — which is why the shape is (1, 5) rather than (1, 7), and why slicing `[1:-1]` off a GPT-2 sequence removes real words. The `Ġ` is byte-level BPE's printable stand-in for a leading space, from 4.8 — **so `Ġcapital` is a different token from `capital`, and the space is carried by the word that follows it.**

d.title: The positional signal is twice the token signal at the input
d.caption: **Token embeddings come in at RMS 0.1077 and position embeddings at 0.2176 — so in a trained GPT-2 the positional contribution is about 2× the token contribution, summing to 0.2418.** Which is the measured answer to the question 4.2 §06 raised from the other side: **the original paper scaled embeddings up by `sqrt(d_model)` to stop position dominating, and here, after training, position dominates anyway** — because learned tables find their own scale and this one chose a larger one.

d.title: The residual stream grows 200-fold and then the final norm pulls it back
d.caption: **RMS goes 0.2418 at the embedding output to 50.9625 at layer 11 — a 211× growth — and then the final LayerNorm brings it to 6.8346.** 4.7 measured 1.29× on an *untrained* stack; this is what training does to the same mechanism. And the attention check confirms the architecture across the whole model: **upper-triangle maximum 0.00e+00 over all 144 head-layer combinations.** The sink is here too: **the final token puts 61% of its layer-0 attention on the first token.**

d.title: All the logits are large and negative, and it does not matter
d.caption: **The raw logit range is [−129.868, −100.250] — every value negative, and softmax is shift-invariant, so only their differences matter.** Which is worth knowing before debugging a model by printing logits: **their absolute level is meaningless.** And the shape is (1, 5, 50257): **one distribution per position from a single pass, of which generation uses only the last, because it is the only position that has attended to the whole prompt.**

d.title: Paris is fifth, at 0.0322, behind “the” at 0.0846
d.caption: **The model's top candidate is `' the'` and `' Paris'` is fifth — and entropy is 5.9985 nats against a maximum of 10.8249, so the distribution is genuinely uncertain rather than wrong.** `'The capital of France is the capital of...'` is a perfectly good continuation. Greedy decoding then shows the consequence: **it takes `' the'`, and from there `' capital'` at 0.1697 and `' of'` at 0.9271** — **each step is locally confident and the path never reaches Paris.**

d.title: Top-p at 0.9 keeps 1,503 tokens; top-k at 50 covers 55% of the mass
d.caption: The two truncations are not comparable settings. **`k=50` keeps 50 tokens covering 0.5495 of the mass; `p=0.90` keeps 1,503 tokens** — because this distribution has a long tail and a fixed `k` cannot know that. Which is the argument for nucleus sampling: **it adapts its size to the shape.** Temperature is orthogonal and does not change the ranking: **at `T=0.1` the top token holds 0.994 and sampling is effectively greedy; at `T=2.0` entropy is 9.4254 against a uniform maximum of 10.8249.**

d.title: Four strategies, four different texts, one prompt
d.caption: **Greedy and beam-4 both loop — `'the capital of France, and the capital of France is the'` — which is 3.4's finding that perplexity rewards repetition, arriving as output.** Sampling escapes the loop and pays for it: **`T=0.7, p=0.9` invents a claim about French culture, and `T=1.5, k=50` runs into `<|endoftext|>` mid-sentence.** The decoded ids are the same eleven integers the whole lesson has been tracking, **so the only thing that differed between these four outputs was how one distribution was sampled.**
